headline: In Blakeman's own Nassau County, Hochul edges ahead by about 1,200 votes
dek: Trump carried Nassau by 4 points in 2024. Two years later, with a quarter fewer ballots cast, the county executive running for governor trailed Kathy Hochul at home by a fraction of a point, a smaller shift than the state's.
summary: Bruce Blakeman's home county, Nassau, moved 4 points left and narrowly favored Kathy Hochul, D+0.2, with counting unfinished.

paras.text: Nassau County is the suburban county between Queens and Suffolk on Long Island. The Census Bureau put its population at 1,398,939 in 2025, and its median household income of about $146,000 is the highest of any county in New York. Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for governor, has run the county since 2022.

In 2024 Donald Trump carried Nassau by 4.2 points out of 706,541 votes. In AP's count of the governor's race, Democrat Kathy Hochul leads Blakeman 266,444 to 265,277. That is a 1,167-vote edge, or D+0.2, with 98.39 percent of the expected vote counted. It amounts to a 4-point move toward the Democrats.

That move was smaller than the state's. New York went from D+12.7 for Kamala Harris to D+19.6 for Hochul, a 7.0-point shift, with 93.04 percent counted. Nassau ranks 17th of New York's 62 counties by move. Only half the state's counties moved left at all. Next door, Suffolk moved 11 points, from R+10.0 to D+0.8. Queens moved 20 points and Westchester 5. Across the country the typical county moved 14 points, and most big suburban counties that leaned Republican in 2024 moved much further than Nassau: Maricopa, Arizona, 20 points; Tarrant, Texas, 24; Hillsborough, Florida, 12. Only Pinellas, Florida, at 6, came close to Nassau's shift.

The result is not final. The uncounted share of the vote is several times larger than Hochul's lead. In New York, absentee, affidavit and military ballots counted after election night are not included, and the county certifies its results weeks later. Local outlets have published different Nassau tallies as the count has gone on.

About 532,000 votes were cast, roughly 174,000 fewer than in 2024 and 75 percent of the presidential turnout. A county-level count cannot separate voters who changed sides from voters who stayed home or turned out. Nassau's 4-point move mixes both.

The Times Union found that Blakeman expected a boost from Long Island's Nassau and Suffolk counties that never materialized. Before the election, Politico reported that Republicans expected his candidacy to turbo charge down-ballot turnout. Jay Jacobs, who leads both the state and Nassau Democratic parties, conceded that Blakeman will have an organization working for him in Nassau County.

Much of the campaign was about Nassau itself. Gothamist reported that Blakeman painted Hochul as soft on crime and immigration, faulting her for signing into law a measure restricting local governments — including Nassau County — from cooperating with federal immigration agents. The newsroom Documented found that Nassau County under Blakeman has handed more immigrants over to ICE than any other county in the state. At their debate, News 12 reported, Hochul criticized ICE operations and called the agency "out of control" in Nassau, while Blakeman defended his county's cooperation with ICE, saying it makes communities safer. Hochul also spent $30 million worth of ads touting her push to send energy rebate checks to New Yorkers, pause data center construction and expand access to childcare. Blakeman pledged to cut income taxes and utility bills. Each candidate also tried to tie the other to a polarizing figure: Hochul linked Blakeman to Trump, who endorsed him. Blakeman went after Hochul's alliance with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
NBC News' exit poll found Long Island voters split evenly between the two candidates, which fits the county counts. No Nassau-only survey has yet shown which voters moved.

The bigger local shift came further down the ballot. In the Town of Hempstead, Democrat Joe Scianablo beat Republican Supervisor John Ferretti, and News 12 noted that the win makes Scianablo just the second Democrat elected Hempstead Town Supervisor in more than a century. Larry Levy of Hofstra University told News 12 that Scianablo will need to work closely with the Republican-majority Town Board. The Long Island Press reported that Democrats also flipped a Nassau state Senate seat, the 6th Senate District, which covers Freeport, Garden City, Hempstead and Mineola, among other communities. Democratic Reps. Tom Suozzi (NY-03) and Laura Gillen (NY-04) have secured reelection. Still, the Herald noted that Republicans held on to several state and county seats.

Blakeman stays where he was. He still has three years left in his second term as executive of Nassau County, and Hochul said she would continue to work with Blakeman on behalf of Nassau County. Nassau Republicans told NBC New York that the loss is only a temporary defeat. The county's numbers suggest a place that is still close: it moved toward the Democrats this year, but by less than New York as a whole, and the final count could still change which candidate carried it.
